title: A predictive causal theory of mammalian aging

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that explains which biological processes cause mammalian aging, how those processes affect one another, and how changing them would alter tissue function and survival. Its defining capability would be quantitative prediction of interventions that were not used to build the theory, within explicitly stated biological limits. It would need to distinguish causes from accompanying changes and identify when an apparently beneficial intervention would fail or create trade-offs. This is the target capability, not an achievement demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

The scientific motivation allows for several interacting causes rather than requiring one universal upstream driver. The supplied 2022 study discusses somatic mutations, telomere attrition, epigenetic drift and loss of proteostasis as proposed contributors whose causal roles and relative contributions remained debated. A theory could therefore involve multiple mechanisms acting at different scales. The source supports that multifactorial motivation, but does not itself establish a complete network of interactions from molecules through cells and tissues to whole-organism aging.

significance.text: Conditional significance: reliable prediction of previously untested intervention effects would give researchers a way to compare competing explanations of aging and prioritize experiments before committing to lengthy intervention studies. Predictions of failure, harm or tissue-specific trade-offs would be valuable alongside predictions of benefit. The direct advance would be an experimentally testable capacity for causal prediction across the theory’s validated range.

The underlying scientific difficulty is illustrated by the supplied paper’s distinction between candidate forms of molecular damage and their uncertain causal contributions. A successful theory could help resolve such competing explanations. However, predictive accuracy alone would not uniquely establish every internal mechanism: different explanations can sometimes produce similar predictions, so targeted tests of the proposed mechanisms would remain necessary.

Conditional downstream possibilities: better intervention selection could make longevity research more efficient and help identify combinations that improve function or survival. Effective human therapies would still require suitable interventions, delivery methods, safety assessment and clinical validation. A theory would not by itself demonstrate human rejuvenation, greatly slowed systemic aging or indefinite lifespan, and success in selected mammals would not guarantee equivalent effects in humans.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is a model that moves from describing age-associated changes to predicting the consequences of deliberately changing their causes. The supplied comparative study leaves a concrete causal question unresolved: even if somatic mutation rates are associated with species lifespan, how much do those mutations contribute to ordinary aging, and would reducing them improve function or extend life? The paper explicitly considers non-causal explanations and calls for studies of mutations and clonal expansions in age-related disease and aging phenotypes.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: a general intervention-predictive theory would need to separate initiating causes from downstream consequences, compensatory responses and correlated markers. It would need to represent interactions among candidate mechanisms and explain why an intervention’s effects vary with tissue, species, age or biological context. Predicting mutation accumulation alone would cover only one component of the intended scope; the theory must connect its proposed causes to functional and survival outcomes.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: building and testing that capability requires measurements and perturbations that can distinguish competing causal explanations. Researchers would need comparable outcomes across tissues and species, interventions sufficiently informative to test mechanisms, explicit treatment of uncertainty, and validation data independent of model construction. Long-term survival outcomes and potentially different effects across tissues make validation demanding. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not a documented inventory of all remaining barriers as of November 2026.

current_state.text: Alex Cagan, Adrian Baez-Ortega and colleagues published “Somatic mutation rates scale with lifespan across mammals” online in Nature on 13 April 2022, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-022-04618-z. They used whole-genome sequencing of 208 intestinal crypts from 56 individuals across 16 mammalian species to study somatic mutations. The lifespan association analysis included the 15 species with age information, a narrower scope than the overall sampling.

The study reported an inverse association between annual somatic mutation rate and species lifespan, consistent with a simple model in which annual mutation rates are inversely proportional to lifespan. This is comparative evidence from intestinal crypts. It does not establish the same relationship throughout every tissue, quantify how much ordinary aging is caused by mutations, or demonstrate that reducing mutation rates extends life. The authors explicitly considered alternative non-causal explanations. The result supplies a clue for causal theories rather than a demonstration of the proposed general capability.

The supplied review verified the article’s identity and assessed relevant text from its main article, methods and end matter. The source index reports a non-truncated extraction with a PDF object-pointer warning, while the review treats the available evidence as partial because extraction issues were recorded and supplementary material and figure images were not inspected. The review found the relevant passages readable despite that warning. The account here relies on those reviewed textual findings; it does not add claims from uninspected figures or supplementary material.

Temporal limitation of the supplied record: the research establishes a dated 2022 result, but the review contains no subsequent search record establishing progress through 1 November 2026. It therefore does not determine whether the target capability remained absent at that date or resolve developments through the source’s retrieval on 11 November 2026. This gap in coverage does not invalidate the concept or show that later progress has or has not occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: preregister quantitative predictions for interventions excluded from model development, across multiple tissues and mammalian species. Include predicted successes, failures and trade-offs, and specify the conditions under which each prediction applies. Before testing, define prediction tolerances, uncertainty estimates, validation datasets and outcome measures. These are proposed assessment criteria, not standards established by the supplied paper.
completion_criteria.label: Preregister quantitative held-out intervention predictions across mammalian tissues and species

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal validation: combine intervention-outcome predictions with experiments that distinguish the theory’s claimed mechanisms from plausible alternatives. Test functional and survival outcomes rather than relying only on changes in a molecular marker. Where the theory attributes an effect to a particular causal pathway, use targeted perturbations and suitable controls to test that attribution. Successful prediction should be accompanied by evidence for the causal explanation it advances.
completion_criteria.label: Experiments distinguish claimed mechanisms underlying functional and survival predictions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: independent groups should confirm important predictions using prespecified protocols and independent data. The theory should explain important exceptions, report failures and identify limits to transfer across tissues, species and intervention classes. Any intended human application would require separate human validation. A finite set of successful tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality across all mammalian aging.
completion_criteria.label: Independent groups reproduce predictions within explicitly reported biological limits

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with LON-02, “Safe, repeatable rejuvenation of an aged human body,” and LON-03, “A validated human intervention that greatly slows systemic aging”: LON-01 concerns explanatory and predictive capability; these entries concern achieved intervention outcomes in humans. A causal theory could guide either effort, but validating the theory would not establish either human outcome. Conversely, a successful intervention could be discovered before a broadly predictive theory exists.

Conceptual comparison with LON-04, “A fast, validated surrogate for human longevity trials”: a surrogate would provide a faster measurement that reliably stands in for a longer-term outcome in a defined setting. A causal theory could help explain when that substitution is justified, while a validated surrogate could accelerate tests of the theory. Predicting a biomarker’s movement is insufficient unless its relationship to relevant outcomes is established within the intended use.

Conceptual comparison with LON-05, “In-place repair of accumulated molecular damage in old tissues”: repair would be a specific intervention capability, whereas LON-01 would aim to predict when repairing particular damage changes aging outcomes. The supplied mutation study illustrates the distinction: an association between damage accumulation and lifespan does not by itself establish the benefit of preventing or repairing that damage.

Conceptual comparison with LON-06, “Transfer of exceptional longevity mechanisms between species”: comparative findings can suggest mechanisms worth investigating, but transferring a mechanism requires showing that it works in a recipient species. LON-01 would seek to predict whether such transfer should work, under what conditions and with what trade-offs. The supplied cross-species mutation-rate association does not demonstrate a transferable longevity mechanism.

Conceptual comparison with LON-07, “Control of systemic aging signals through the circulation”: circulation-mediated effects could form one component of a broader causal theory and provide interventions with which to test it. LON-07 concerns control of a particular route of systemic influence; LON-01 seeks predictions across consequential mechanisms, including their interactions and limits. Neither capability automatically establishes the other.

Disciplinary synthesis: LON-01 overlaps with causal inference, systems biology, comparative genomics and experimental intervention research. Those fields contribute methods and evidence, while the defining target remains prediction of aging intervention outcomes across a stated mammalian scope. These overlaps do not merge the distinct innovations in the supplied roster.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish subsequent progress after the 2022 study or whether the target capability remained absent as of 1 November 2026.
The causal contribution of somatic mutations to ordinary aging, and whether reducing them would improve function or extend lifespan, remain unresolved by the supplied study.
The supplied evidence does not establish how the intestinal-crypt findings generalize across tissues or explain the relative contributions and interactions of other candidate aging mechanisms.

A future demonstration protocol still needs concrete prediction tolerances, validation datasets, intervention coverage, outcome definitions and criteria for distinguishing competing causal mechanisms.
Supplementary material and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review. The recorded extraction warning and partial review coverage limit claims beyond the reviewed text.
